title: Dense Subgraph Discovery Meets Strong Triadic Closure

problem.claim: The paper studies dense subgraph discovery while accounting for unequal connection strengths through strong triadic closure labelings.

gap.claim: Existing dense subgraph discovery is extended to a setting where strong triadic closure labelings are not unique and jointly selecting a subgraph and labeling is computationally difficult.

contributions.claim: The paper formulates a score for a subgraph and strong triadic closure labeling as a weighted ratio of strong and weak edges to the number of nodes, with user parameter λ, and seeks to maximize it.
The formulation specializes to densest subgraph discovery when λ = 1 and largest clique when λ = 0, implying NP-hardness.
The paper proposes an exact integer-linear-programming algorithm and four practical polynomial-time heuristics.

author_reported_evidence.claim: An extensive experimental study reports that the algorithms find the ground truth in synthetic datasets.
The experimental study reports efficient execution on real-world datasets.

narrative_sequence.summary: Dense subgraph discovery has applications, but network connections may have unequal strength.
Strong triadic closure labels edges as strong or weak and imposes a connectivity condition on pairs sharing a strong neighbor.
Strong triadic closure labelings are non-unique, and maximizing strong edges is NP-hard.
The paper applies strong triadic closure to dense subgraph discovery and defines a parameterized score to maximize over subgraphs and labelings.
The formulation connects to densest subgraph and largest clique at parameter extremes, followed by an exact algorithm, four heuristics, and an experimental study.

source_observation.claim: The parameter λ interpolates between densest subgraph discovery at λ = 1 and largest clique at λ = 0.

interpretation.claim: A tunable objective can expose relationships between different graph optimization problems.

application.claim: When designing graph objectives, examine limiting parameter values to identify familiar special cases and computational boundaries.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that intermediate λ values provide better outcomes for any particular application.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the integer-linear-programming formulation.
The abstract does not describe the four heuristics.
The abstract does not provide dataset sizes, runtime measurements, or experimental baselines.
The abstract does not define the ground truth used in the synthetic experiments.
